title: The Interpreter
author: Léxi
desc: Salimata est interprète lors d'un grand sommet à Abidjan. Pendant trois jours, elle prête sa voix à un diplomate anglais. Mais que se passe-t-il quand on traduit les mots de quelqu'un… et qu'on finit par les penser ?

p: For three days every year, Salimata Bakayoko disappeared. Not physically — she sat in a small glass booth at the back of the conference hall at the Sofitel Ivoire, headphones over her ears, microphone in front of her mouth — but her own voice, her own opinions, her own personality, vanished completely. For three days, she became other people.

She was a conference interpreter, one of the best in West Africa. When a minister from Nigeria spoke English, it was Salimata's voice that the French-speaking delegates heard, translating in real time, a second or two behind him. She had been the voice of presidents, bankers, scientists and, once, a rather famous footballer who swore in four languages.
"The secret," her old teacher in Geneva used to say, "is to be invisible. A good interpreter is a window. Nobody looks at a window. They look through it."
This year's summit was about climate and agriculture. Salimata had studied the vocabulary for weeks: drought resilience, carbon credits, crop rotation. She was ready for anything.
She was not ready for the British delegate.

chapters.t: The Man Who Spoke Too Fast
p: His name was Daniel Okafor-Hughes. He was perhaps thirty-five, half Nigerian, half English, and he spoke faster than anyone Salimata had ever interpreted. Worse, he improvised. He abandoned his written speech after the first paragraph and began to talk — passionately, with jokes and sudden silences — about his grandmother's farm near Enugu, about the year the rains failed, about a cousin who had crossed the Sahara looking for work and never come back.

Salimata followed him, breathless. She chose her words in fractions of a second, matched his rhythm, caught his jokes and, somehow, his emotion too. In the hall, the French-speaking delegates laughed at the right moments. Some of them wiped their eyes.
When the session ended, she took off her headphones, exhausted and strangely shaken.
Someone knocked on the glass of the booth. It was him.
"I'm sorry," he said, smiling apologetically. "I'm told I'm an interpreter's worst nightmare. I wanted to thank you. A colleague said that in French, I sounded better than I do in English."
"That's not true," said Salimata, before she could stop herself. "You sounded exactly like you."
It was the first sentence she had spoken in her own voice all day.
They had dinner on the second evening, at a small maquis by the lagoon that Salimata chose because no delegate would ever find it. They talked until the waiter started stacking chairs around them.

He told her he had become a diplomat almost by accident, because he spoke four languages and was too stubborn to stay quiet in meetings. She told him she had become an interpreter because, as a shy child in Bouaké, she had discovered that she could say anything at all as long as it was someone else's words.
"So you've never said what you think," he said. "Professionally."
"Never. That's the job."
"Doesn't it bother you? Giving your voice to people you disagree with?"

She thought about it honestly. "Sometimes. Last year, I interpreted a man who said terrible things about migrants. I translated every word perfectly. Then I went to the bathroom and was sick." She shrugged. "But a window doesn't choose what people see."
Daniel looked at her for a long moment across the candle.
"You're not a window," he said. "Windows don't get sick."
On the final morning, everything went wrong.

The head of Daniel's delegation fell ill, and Daniel was asked to deliver the closing statement — a carefully negotiated text, approved by London, full of vague promises and comfortable words. Salimata had a copy in the booth. She had read it twice. It said, essentially, nothing.
Daniel stood at the podium and read the first page in a flat, obedient voice. Salimata translated it in the same tone.
Then he stopped. He looked at the room for a long time. He folded the paper.

"I'm sorry," he said. "I can't read the rest of this. It's very elegant. But last night someone told me that a person who repeats words he doesn't believe is just a window. And I would rather be something else."
In the booth, Salimata's hand froze above the microphone. For one terrible second, she didn't speak. Six hundred delegates waited in silence for the French.
Then she leaned in, and she translated every word — including those.
Daniel went on to speak for fifteen minutes, without notes, about what richer countries actually owed to farmers in the Sahel. It was not diplomatic. It was the best speech of the summit.
He was recalled to London two days later. The newspapers called his speech "undiplomatic" and "remarkable" in the same sentence. His career survived, just.
He wrote to her every week. Long letters, by email but written like real letters, in an English full of jokes and sudden silences. She answered in French. Neither of them translated.

Six months later, Salimata stood in front of a microphone again — not in a booth this time, but on a stage at the university in Bouaké, in front of three hundred students. They had invited her to talk about her profession.
She had prepared a speech. It was very elegant. She looked at it, then at the faces in front of her, and folded the paper.
"For twelve years," she said, "my job was to disappear. I was very good at it. Today, I'd like to try something different. I'd like to tell you what I think."
She spoke for forty minutes. In the third row, a tall man who had flown in from London that morning without telling her listened to every word, and did not need an interpreter at all.
